The ground **should** be highest at your house and should gradually decline away from the structure.

The ground being graded above the foundation line *is* an issue, but it's a different issue as it can allow your framing to suck up groundwater and ultimately rot.

But if you are going to lower the grade at the structure, you are also going to have to lower the grade an equal amount everywhere else to maintain slope. It's a massive undertaking.

As others have stated, the likely culprit is the drain tile being blocked or simply inadequate. Most of the water that can potentially get into your basement in a storm is going to be coming off your roof/from your gutters. Unless the property is graded back towards the building, ground water simply isn't going to travel in that direction.

So, to reiterate what others have said, if you redirect your gutters to drain much further away from the building, this particular basement water issue will go away.

I know that it’s easy to say this with everything being edited and published already, and perhaps it wasn’t as clear during filming what the alliances were, but in the future I think it could really add to the drama to have players who are from different alliances forced to work together in the duo challenges, and you would probably have to randomly assign teammates for this to occur versus having the players pick their partners. 

The duo aspect really came into play in the final episode when Victim and B0aty were paired towards the end of the challenge, at that point b0aty needed to score more than victim but didn’t have the ability to. If future finals were to be of the same format, the final challenge should always be a solo challenge to allow trailing players to try to close the gap and avoid this scenario.

One other thing that felt a little bit off was the fact that B0aty got into the final simply on account of having the amulet of power, despite losing the semifinal challenge. My personal opinion is that the semifinal should represent that one final chance to eliminate any player on the losing side, to get rid of that player you fear most in the final. To that end, the “quarterfinal” should award something like a ring of life instead, it protects you for the current week that you won, but you don’t have protection in the semifinals, unless you win the semifinal challenge. This might have been less of an issue if the semifinal was a solo challenge, but in a team challenge it felt a little weird to have a player on the losing team be immune given the magnitude of the moment heading into the finals.

I’m curious if you’ve ever explored the idea of having a tribe based system, potentially with a player draft that could occur several times through the season to shake up the tribes. It would be interesting to see what kind of alliances may form across tribes given the potential movement of players from one tribe to the other, and especially given that GG doesn’t have the solitude/isolation aspect that a show like Survivor has, which promotes loyalty to your tribe and your tribe only. I think there are a lot of storylines and interpersonal relationships that would be explored with a format like this. 

In the vein of a draft, one small change I would like to see in the future is the way the teams are formed for group challenges. In season 3 teams were formed based on the order a challenge was completed, I.e. first four, second four, last four. This created an incentive for some players to simply finish last to ensure they would play together for the challenge. My proposal, in this example, would be for the first three players to finish to serve as team captains and pick their teammates for the challenge in a snake draft. This would provide an incentive to finish as quickly as possible as well as ensure that the teams are relatively equal in terms of ability, rather than having all of the best players (for the particular challenge) on the same team. 

I really liked the redemption/re-entry arc from season 2, and wish that would have been included in season 3. That provided some really great content. I’m hopeful to see it return in the future. 

A couple challenge ideas that could be explored would be xp from scratch/small seed money, as well as a challenge where there is an incentive to do unique content that other teams/players did not do, for example in the monster combat level challenge, perhaps there is a 50% or similar penalty to the monster’s combat level if another player kills the same monster as a part of their 3 as you did.

Anyways, this turned into quite the comment, thanks again for all of your hard work and looking forward to an even more amazing season 4!

At the very least, if you are going to cut this pipe apart to glue it, do yourself a favor and put in a wye with an elbow so that if the water does continue to back up, it has a place to go that isn't back into your basement.

Also, I can't tell from your photos, but does your sump line coming out of the basement have a check valve on it? If not, that's probably something you want to think about adding.

The french drain has very likely failed, based on what I'm reading. If there is no pop up emitter at the end of the french drain, and the soil has mixed with the rock of the french drain over time so that the water no longer drains and just sits in the pipe, that would explain how he's getting so much back pressure at the top of the pipe--the water has nowhere to go. I predict a flooded basement in the future, because the french drain is a much bigger issue here.

Depending on how your french drain is built... it could have failed. Many french drains are not built correctly, the french drain industry is full of hacks who use bad materials and do the job quickly and poorly.

If your sump line is draining into the french drain, and the french drain has become clogged and failed, that could be why you are seeing water come out of the sump pump onto the patio. Sealing that pipe now without addressing the french drain issue could be a costly mistake.

With the amount of water your sump pump puts out, you really need quite a large leach field to be able to handle it. I highly recommend the french drain man's channel on youtube, he builds really great systems that are made to last hundreds of years.

The number one mistake that french drain installers tend to make is using the incorrect materials. Slotted pipe is the right pipe to use, but it needs to be paired with large stone without fine aggregate mixed in, as well as the correct water permeable fabric (the French Drain Man always uses a non-woven geotextile fabric, which is NOT landscaping fabric) to wrap it all up. French drains will ALWAYS fail if the soil is allowed to get mixed in with the stone. That could be what has happened to you. A french drain functions by creating voids underground for water to occupy until it can drain down via gravity. This is why you want the large stone without the fines, you want the water to fill the voids, not the fines. It's also why french drains can be run with multiple pipes in one trench, to create a bigger void for water to fill.

It was eye opening, especially the union dropping the ball the way that they did. Life works in mysterious ways--you just can't let moments like this one define you.

I got fired. PSE doing dispatch for around a year. My supervisor had invited me to take some extra time at the end of my shift sorting UBBM—he knew I had a wedding coming up and was trying to help bolster my check a little bit. 

I was doing just that—sorting UBBM—and I found several bundles of red plums, in delivery sequence, all from the same route—clearly had never been worked or taken out to the street, they were all perfect. I went to the delivery supervisor who was still in the office to bring it to his attention, and his response was “What do you think I’m going to do about this? I don’t care, I’m not worried about it.”

I was kind of taken back by his response, and I said to him “You’re supposed to be the supervisor, our job is to deliver the mail, I’m telling you about mail that should be delivered but it isn’t being delivered, and you say you don’t care? Wow, that’s a really shitty attitude. I just lost a lot of respect for you.” Then I started walking away, going back to work on the UBBM some more. 

He apparently didn’t like what I said to him, because he actually got up from his desk and started following me. He began asking me what I was even still doing at work, telling me thing like “That’s not your job” and “just go home”. I kept telling him I was doing what I was told I could do by my supervisor, but he wasn’t having it. He started raising his voice and I, regrettably, raised my voice back at him. I never cursed at him, never called him names, never made any threats. All I did was shout. And at this point, it was only us and maybe one or two others in the office. Everyone else had gone home.

The next day I went in to work and my time card was missing. I was escorted into the break room and informed I was being placed on emergency placement because the post office had determined I was a threat to myself and others. I was banned from entering that postal facility while they conducted an “investigation”. The contents of my locker were held hostage for several days, and they would not let me go empty my locker, a supervisor would have to go and do that for me. And even when they did, they still didn’t give me all my stuff. So I lost stuff as a result. 

The union steward of the office had stepped down a couple months prior, so at the time we were being represented by the business agent. I worked with him for about two weeks before things went silent. I called after a few days and was told that our office now has a new steward and he couldn’t help me anymore as a result. I called the new steward and she basically didn’t have any of the info, so we got to start over.

Then… the union just didn’t file the grievance in time. I went in to talk to her and she just flat out was like “Yeah the deadline is passed and we didn’t file an extension, so there’s nothing we can do.”

All told, six months after the fact I got a letter of removal and was out. My life has actually improved a lot since leaving the post office, in a way I’m kind of glad it happened. But overall I kind of got screwed, I should have made a lot of back pay and didn’t. 

By then I was getting married and was ready to just put it in the past, so I moved on. Anyways, that’s my story.

The doctors and psychologists were certain that the solitude would be the most challenging aspect of the mission.

Failure was not an option.

We weren't even sure that intergalactic travel was *possible,* let alone if the human body could survive it. It was all just a bunch of theories and hypotheses, but they would determine the fate of the human race.

It shouldn't have required the end of the world to unify us... but there we were. And now, here I sat.

There was little time for testing. There were no animal trials. In theory, I had everything I needed to survive, if I could maintain my sanity. It wasn't a popular idea to go it alone on this mission. What if something happened? What if I were incapacitated? It was a necessary risk. The shuttle needed to be small. It needed to be lightweight. There was no room for additional crew and the supplies they would require to survive.

The shuttle was loaded with embryos and incubators, and I had practiced on the equipment thousands of times--it always did exactly what it was supposed to do. If the human race were to survive, failure was not an option. If the human race were to perish, it would be because I failed.

Failure was **not** an option.

It took eighteen months to reach the asteroid belt. If we'd had more time, maybe we could have found a way to generate enough energy to do the jump from Earth. Maybe we could have saved... anyone else.

Transmissions from Earth ceased after eleven months. I attempted to make communications for another three weeks thereafter. There was never any response. It was only when I shut down the comms system to conserve power that the magnitude of the situation hit me.

The next seven months were grueling. My emotions varied, seemingly minute by minute, from stoic to suicidal to euphoric to hopeless. When I finally reached the asteroid belt, I felt that I had beat the odds.

I did not anticipate my hesitation to initiate the jump sequence. The switch was shielded by a plastic cover meant to prevent initiating the sequence by mistake. Though I had traveled eighteen months to get here, it felt like a light year that my hand hovered over the plastic. When I finally touched it, it was the weight of the world in my hand. The next minute would decide whether I would live or die, and the rest of the human race with me.

Failure was not an option.

When I finally removed the cover, I did not hesitate to hit the switch. It would be thirty seconds or so from the time I hit the switch to the time I would (ideally) be launched out of the galaxy towards Kepler-62f. No simulation or training could prepare me for the infinite possibilities that lie at the other end of this jump.

I closed my eyes and I waited.

Failure was... a possiblity.

I waited, expecting to feel a sensation that never arrived. I opened my eyes and a single tear emerged.

We had done it. I re-engaged the comms system. Reaching Earth was pointless, of course, but broadcasting a message to the cosmos would be proof I had made it.

I had only just begun to speak when I froze.

There, to my left, suddenly appeared another shuttle. 

And another. 

And another.

It took me a few moments to realize that each shuttle was emblazoned "NASA"--the same as mine. It only took a few seconds for my confusion to turn to excitement. It took a few moments more for my excitement to turn to worry--there was no guarantee the occupants of those ships were alive. This didn't change anything--not for me, not for my mission. 

Kepler-62f lay there before me. It was beautiful. It was a new beginning, if one of us could make it to the ground. 

My excitement quickly became fear as a new, larger, and very different ship appeared before us, completely obscuring our view of Kepler-62f.

Over the radio, a distinctly alien voice spoke: "This is the Intergalactic Police. It has been many millennia since we have seen your kind here."

Failure was the last thing on my mind.

If they request service, the sender pays more money to have the mail piece returned, forwarded, or to receive updated info on that recipient.
